subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 6! Look around you right now and you are surrounded by 3D shapes. The book on the table is a cuboid. The tin of tomatoes in the kitchen is a cylinder. A die from a board game is a cube, and a ball for football is a sphere. Everything you can pick up and hold, everything that takes up space and casts a shadow, is a three-dimensional shape. In this unit you will learn to look at these solid objects the way a mathematician does – to name them, to describe their parts exactly, and to understand how they are built.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 5 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: This unit is designed for self-paced learning. That means you move at your own speed. Read each explanation slowly, try every worked example yourself on paper, and only move on when you feel ready. Your AI tutor is available day and night to explain a step in a new way, give you extra practice, or check your answers. Your teacher will also meet with you about twice a week to help with anything that feels tricky. The most helpful thing of all in this unit is to have real objects beside you – a box, a tin, a die, a ball. Pick them up, turn them over, and count their parts with your own hands.

Why does this matter? When Yusuf helps his family pack goods into boxes at the Hargeisa market, he is thinking about how solid shapes fit together. When Khadija folds a flat sheet of card into a small box for dates at Eid, she is using a net. When an architect in Mogadishu designs a building, or an engineer plans a water tank, they must understand faces, edges and volume. Spatial thinking – the ability to picture and turn shapes in your mind – is one of the most valuable skills you can build, and it starts right here.
Explain the difference between 2D and 3D shapes and give real examples of each.
Name common 3D shapes: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere, prism and pyramid.
Identify and count the faces, edges and vertices of a 3D shape.
Describe the special properties of a cube (6 square faces, 12 equal edges, 8 vertices).
Understand what a net is and identify which nets fold into a cube.
Draw 3D shapes on isometric paper and show which faces are visible and which are hidden.
Recognise that the same shape looks different from different viewpoints.
Find the volume of a cube or cuboid by counting or multiplying unit cubes.

concepts.title: What Makes a Shape 3D?
concepts.explanation:
A 2D shape, or two-dimensional shape, is completely flat. Think of a square drawn on paper. It has length (how long it is) and width (how wide it is), but no thickness at all. You can only ever see it from one side, because there is no other side to see. Circles, triangles, rectangles and pentagons are all 2D shapes. They live on the flat surface of the page.

A 3D shape, or three-dimensional shape, is solid. It has length and width like a 2D shape, but it also has a third measurement: height or depth. This third dimension is what lets a shape take up space in the real world. Because a 3D shape is solid, you can look at it from many directions – the front, the side, the top, the bottom – and it may look different from each. You can hold it, walk around it, and even fit things inside it.

Here is a simple way to feel the difference. Draw a square on paper: that is 2D. Now pick up a die: that is a cube, the 3D version of a square. The square has become a solid box with a front, a back, a top, a bottom and two sides. A very common mistake is to call a flat square a 'cube' – but a cube is solid and has six square faces, while a square is just one flat shape. Whenever you are unsure, ask yourself: can I pick it up and hold it? If yes, it is 3D. If it lives only on the paper, it is 2D.
concepts.example: 3D shapes are all around your home and your town. The wall of the masjid is part of a giant cuboid. A tin of camel milk is a cylinder. An ice-cream cone is, of course, a cone. A mango is close to a sphere, and the great pyramids that people build are pyramids. Learning to spot these shapes in the world is the first step to understanding them, and once you start noticing, you will see them everywhere you look.

concepts.title: Faces, Edges and Vertices
concepts.explanation:
Every 3D shape is built from three kinds of parts, and a mathematician can describe any solid by counting them. These three parts are faces, edges and vertices, and they are the vocabulary you will use for the rest of this unit.

A face is a flat surface of the shape – like one whole side of a box. Faces are the parts you could paint.

An edge is a straight line where two faces meet – like the sharp line along the side of a book.

A vertex is a corner point where three or more edges meet – the pointy corners of the shape. The plural of vertex is vertices.

Let us look at a cube to see all three at once. Pick up a die if you have one. The flat squares you can see are the faces – there are 6 of them. Run your finger along one of the sharp lines between two squares: that is an edge, and a cube has 12 of them. Now touch one of the pointed corners where the edges meet: that is a vertex, and a cube has 8. So a cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. Saying this out loud while touching a real die makes it stick in your memory far better than reading it alone.

Counting these parts sounds easy, but it is where many learners slip. The trouble is that some faces, edges and vertices are hidden round the back where you cannot see them. If you only count the parts facing you, you will miss the rest. The safe method is to be systematic: count the top, then the bottom, then go around the sides in order, keeping track so you never count the same part twice and never skip one. For a cube you might count faces as 'top 1, bottom 2, front 3, back 4, left 5, right 6'.
concepts.example: There is a beautiful pattern that connects these three numbers, discovered by a mathematician named Euler (say it 'Oiler'). For any solid with flat faces, if you take the number of vertices, subtract the number of edges, and add the number of faces, you always get 2. We write it as V − E + F = 2. For a cube: 8 − 12 + 6 = 2. It works! This little rule is a wonderful way to check your counting: if your three numbers do not give 2, you have miscounted somewhere and should count again.

concepts.title: The Cube in Detail
concepts.explanation:
The cube is the most important 3D shape to know well, so we will study it closely. A cube is a special solid where every face is an identical square. Because all six faces are the same square, a cube looks the same whichever way you turn it – that is what makes it so neat and useful.

The full list of cube properties is worth learning by heart:

It has 6 faces, and every single one is a square of the same size.

It has 12 edges, and every single one is exactly the same length.

It has 8 vertices, and they all look identical.

Every corner is a right angle of 90 degrees.

Cubes are everywhere in design and technology because these properties make them so practical. Dice are cubes because a cube is fair – it is just as likely to land on any of its six faces. Storage boxes and containers are cube-like because cubes stack neatly and pack together with no wasted space between them. Building blocks, sugar cubes, ice cubes and the blocks in the video game Minecraft are all cubes for the same reasons: they sit still without rolling and they fit together perfectly.

Compare a cube with a sphere for a moment. A ball is lovely to roll, but try to build a wall from footballs and they roll away and leave big gaps. Now build a wall from cube-shaped blocks and it stands firm with no gaps at all. This is exactly why builders, packers and toy-makers reach for cubes and cuboids so often. When Hassan helps stack boxes of dates for transport from Berbera, the boxes are cuboids precisely because they will not roll and they waste no space in the lorry.
concepts.example: Here is a small piece of cube arithmetic you can already do. Because all 12 edges of a cube are the same length, you can find the total length of all the edges by multiplying. If each edge of a cube is 5 cm long, then all the edges together measure 12 × 5 = 60 cm. Little calculations like this show how the properties of a shape lead straight into useful sums.

concepts.title: A Family of 3D Shapes
concepts.explanation:
The cube is just one member of a whole family of solids. Let us meet the others, because each has its own faces, edges and vertices, and its own uses in the world.

A cuboid, also called a rectangular prism, is like a cube that has been stretched. Its 6 faces are rectangles rather than squares, and opposite faces match each other. A cuboid has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices – the same counts as a cube, but the faces need not be equal. Books, smartphones, cereal boxes and bricks are all cuboids. In fact, a cube is really a special cuboid where every face happens to be a square.

A triangular prism has two triangular faces at its ends and three rectangular faces along its sides. It has 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices. You have seen this shape in a Toblerone chocolate bar, in the ridge of a tent, and in the sloping roof of a house. A prism in general is a solid that has the same shape all the way along its length, like a loaf you could slice into identical pieces – which is why a cube and a cuboid are also prisms.

A square-based pyramid has one square base and four triangular faces that lean inwards to meet at a single point at the top called the apex. It has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices. The great pyramids of Egypt are the most famous example. Notice how a pyramid is different from a prism: a prism keeps the same width along its length, but a pyramid narrows to a point.

Three more shapes have curved surfaces, so we describe them a little differently. A cylinder, like a tin of milk, has two flat circular faces and one curved surface that wraps around. A cone, like an ice-cream cone, has one flat circular face and one curved surface that rises to a point. A sphere, like a ball or a ripe mango, is perfectly round with no flat faces at all – which is exactly why it rolls so easily and cannot be stacked.

concepts.title: Nets – Unfolding a Solid
concepts.explanation:
A net is a flat pattern that you can cut out and fold up to make a 3D shape. Here is the best way to picture it: imagine carefully unfolding a cardboard box until it lies completely flat on the table. That flat pattern of joined-up faces is the net of the box. Fold it back along the creases and it becomes a solid again. Every 3D shape with flat faces can be opened out into a net.

Nets matter because they show the link between the flat 2D world and the solid 3D world. The number of shapes in a net tells you the number of faces on the solid. The net of a cube has 6 squares, because a cube has 6 square faces. The net of a cuboid has 6 rectangles. The net of a triangular prism has 2 triangles and 3 rectangles. When Maryam wants to build a small box, she first draws its net, then cuts and folds – exactly what factories do to make the packaging for everything you buy.

But here is the important catch: not every arrangement of 6 squares will fold into a cube. The squares must be joined in the right way, so that when you fold along the edges each square becomes a different face with none overlapping and none missing. A famous cube net is the cross or plus shape: a row of four squares with one square above and one square below the second square in the row. Fold the four in the row into a ring of sides, then fold the top square down as the lid and the bottom square up as the base, and you have a cube.

There are actually eleven different nets that fold into a cube – the cross is only the most common one. Others look like a staircase of squares, or a long strip with squares stepping off the sides. If you ever want to know whether a mystery arrangement of 6 squares is a valid cube net, the surest test is to think like a scientist: draw it, cut it out, and try to fold it. Mathematicians call this specialising – testing a specific example to find out for certain – and then classifying, sorting the patterns into 'these fold into a cube' and 'these do not'.
concepts.example: One more useful idea is the open cube. An open cube is a cube with one face missing – like a box without a lid, or a cup. Its net has only 5 squares instead of 6. Open-cube nets are used for real containers such as storage boxes, drawers and trays. If someone gives you a net of only 5 squares and asks whether it makes a closed cube, the answer is no: a closed cube always needs exactly 6 faces.

concepts.title: Drawing Solids and Seeing Different Views
concepts.explanation:
Drawing a solid shape on flat paper is a real challenge, because you must create the illusion that the shape has depth when the paper itself is flat. This is exactly what artists, architects and designers do every day, and there is a clever tool that makes it much easier: isometric paper.

Isometric paper is covered with dots or lines arranged in a triangular pattern. Ordinary squared paper helps you draw flat squares and rectangles; isometric paper helps you draw cubes and cuboids that look solid. To draw a cube on it, you start at one vertex, draw the three edges that meet there following the slanted grid lines, and then complete the faces you can see. On isometric paper a square face is drawn as a slanted diamond, and this slant is what tricks the eye into seeing depth.

When you look at a solid shape, you can only ever see some of its parts at once; the rest are hidden round the back. For a cube sitting on a table, you can usually see three faces at a time – perhaps the top, the front and one side. The other three faces – the bottom, the back and the far side – are hidden behind the ones you can see. This is why you can never draw all six faces of a cube in a single realistic picture, and it is a favourite exam question. The most faces of a cube you can ever see at once is three.

The same solid shape can look completely different depending on where you stand. Think of a triangular prism lying like a tent. From the front, looking straight at the triangular end, you see a triangle. From the side, you see a rectangle. From directly above, looking down, you also see a rectangle. Turning the shape, or walking around it, changes which faces point towards you and therefore changes what you see. A cube viewed from straight above shows a single square; a cylinder viewed from the side shows a rectangle, but from the end shows a circle.
concepts.example: This is why architects and engineers never rely on just one drawing. To describe a building fully they use several views: a plan (the view from directly above, like a map of the floor), and elevations (the views from the front and the sides). Together these flat views capture a solid object completely. When you learn to imagine a shape from a viewpoint you are not actually standing at, you are using spatial reasoning – one of the most valuable thinking skills in all of mathematics.

methods.title: How to count faces, edges and vertices
methods.example: A triangular prism sits on the table. How many faces, edges and vertices does it have?
steps: Count the faces in a fixed order: top, bottom, then around the sides.
Count the edges the same careful way, including the hidden ones.
Count the vertices (corner points) last.
Check with Euler's rule: V − E + F should equal 2.

methods.title: How to find the volume of a cuboid
methods.example: A cuboid-shaped box of dates is 6 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high. What is its volume?
steps: Write down the length, the width and the height.
Multiply length × width to find the cubes in one layer.
Multiply that by the height to count all the layers.
Give the answer in cubic units (cm³ or m³).

methods.title: How to test a cube net
methods.example: A net is made of four squares in a row, with one square attached above the second square and one square attached below the second square. Will it fold into a cube?
steps: Count the squares – a cube net needs exactly 6.
Imagine folding: four squares curl into the sides, one is the top, one is the bottom.
Check that no two squares would overlap and none is missing.
When unsure, cut it out and fold it to be certain.

methods.title: Hidden faces
methods.example: Omar looks at a cube and can see the top face, the front face and the right side face. Which faces are hidden?
steps: Solution: A cube has 6 faces.
If Omar can see the top, front and right, then the hidden faces are the ones directly opposite each of those: the bottom, the back and the left side.
You can never see more than 3 faces of a cube at once, and each visible face hides the one opposite it.

methods.title: Volume of a cuboid
methods.example: A cuboid box is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 2 cm high. What is its volume?
steps: Solution: Use volume = length × width × height.
That is 5 × 4 × 2.
Work it in steps: 5 × 4 = 20, and 20 × 2 = 40.
The volume is 40 cm³.

methods.title: Packing small cubes
methods.example: How many small cubes with 2 cm edges fit inside a large cube with 6 cm edges?
steps: Solution: Along one edge, 6 ÷ 2 = 3 small cubes fit.
The same is true along all three directions, so the box holds 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 small cubes.
This is the same as finding how many unit blocks build the big shape.

workedExamples.title: Count faces, edges and vertices
workedExamples.prompt: A triangular prism sits on the table. How many faces, edges and vertices does it have?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Count in order. Faces: the two triangular ends make 2, and the three rectangular sides make 3, giving 2 + 3 = 5 faces. Edges: each triangle has 3 edges (2 triangles = 6) plus 3 edges joining the ends, giving 6 + 3 = 9 edges. Vertices: each triangular end has 3 corners, and 3 + 3 = 6 vertices. Check with Euler: 6 − 9 + 5 = 2. Correct!

workedExamples.title: Use Euler's rule to check
workedExamples.prompt: Amina counts a square-based pyramid and says it has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices. Is her counting right?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Test with Euler's rule, V − E + F. That is 5 − 8 + 5 = 2. Because the answer is 2, her counting is consistent and correct. A square pyramid does indeed have 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices.

workedExamples.title: Which net folds into a cube?
workedExamples.prompt: A net is made of four squares in a row, with one square attached above the second square and one square attached below the second square. Will it fold into a cube?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: First count the squares: there are 6 in total, which is the right number for a cube. This is the classic cross-shaped net: as you fold along each seam, the row of four squares wraps around to become the four side faces, the square above folds down to become the top, and the square below folds up to become the bottom. No two squares overlap and none is missing, so yes — this net folds into a closed cube.

workedExamples.title: Hidden faces
workedExamples.prompt: Omar looks at a cube and can see the top face, the front face and the right side face. Which faces are hidden?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: A cube has 6 faces. If Omar can see the top, front and right, then the hidden faces are the ones directly opposite each of those: the bottom, the back and the left side. You can never see more than 3 faces of a cube at once, and each visible face hides the one opposite it.

workedExamples.title: Volume of a cuboid
workedExamples.prompt: A cuboid box is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 2 cm high. What is its volume?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Use volume = length × width × height. That is 5 × 4 × 2. Work it in steps: 5 × 4 = 20, and 20 × 2 = 40. The volume is 40 cm³. You can picture it as two layers, each holding 5 × 4 = 20 unit cubes.

workedExamples.title: Packing small cubes
workedExamples.prompt: How many small cubes with 2 cm edges fit inside a large cube with 6 cm edges?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Along one edge, 6 ÷ 2 = 3 small cubes fit. The same is true along all three directions, so the box holds 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 small cubes. This is the same as finding how many unit blocks build the big shape.

workedExamples.title: Different views
workedExamples.prompt: Zahra looks at a cylinder (a tin of milk). What 2D shape does she see from the side, and what does she see from directly above?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: From the side, the curved surface appears flattened into a rectangle. From directly above, looking down on the round lid, she sees a circle. The same solid gives two very different flat views, which is why more than one view is needed to describe a shape fully.

workedExamples.title: Total edge length of a cube
workedExamples.prompt: A cube has edges that are 7 cm long. What is the total length of all its edges added together?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: A cube has 12 equal edges. If each is 7 cm, the total is 12 × 7 = 84 cm. Because every edge of a cube is the same length, one multiplication does the whole job.

workedExamples.title: What 2D shape do you see from
workedExamples.prompt: What 2D shape do you see from: a) a cube from above b) a cylinder from the side c) a cylinder from the end?
workedExamples.solution: a) square, b) rectangle, c) circle.

activities.title: 3D Shape Treasure Hunt
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and your eyes.
steps: Walk through your home and find one real example of each shape: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere.
For each object, draw a quick picture and write where you found it.
Count and record its faces, edges and vertices.
Make a chart sorting all your objects by shape. Which shape did you find most often?
Keep your chart – it shows how common 3D shapes are in everyday life.

activities.materials: squared paper or card, scissors, tape, colouring pencils.
steps: Draw the cross-shaped cube net: a row of four squares with one square above and one below the second square.
Cut it out carefully and fold along every line to make a closed cube. Tape the edges.
Now design two more nets of 6 squares that you think will fold into a cube, and test them.
Record which nets worked and which did not. For the ones that failed, explain why.
There are eleven different nets that fold into a cube – see how many you can discover!

activities.title: Build a Cube from Unit Cubes (Volume Game)
activities.materials: small identical cubes – dice, sugar cubes, or paper cubes you make.
steps: Build one flat layer that is 3 cubes long and 2 cubes wide. Count the cubes in the layer.
Stack a second and third identical layer on top. Count the total number of cubes.
Check your count using the rule length × width × height.
Challenge a family member (or your AI tutor) to build a secret cuboid and work out its volume.

activities.title: Different Views Investigation
activities.materials: a tin, a box, and a ball.
steps: Place the tin on the table. Draw what it looks like from the side, then from directly above.
Do the same for the box: draw the front view, the side view and the top view.
Ask someone – or your AI tutor – to describe an object by its views only, without naming it, and see if you can guess the shape.
Talk about why an architect needs more than one view to describe a building.

activities.title: Shape Property Quiz Game (Family Game)
activities.materials: your family or friends, and small slips of paper.
steps: On each slip, write a shape clue such as 'I have 6 square faces' or 'I have no flat faces'.
Take turns drawing a slip and naming the shape it describes.
Score a point for each correct answer. The clues can mention faces, edges or vertices.
Make the game harder by adding clues about nets and volume.

activities.title: Design and Build a Box
activities.materials: card, a ruler, scissors and tape.
steps: Decide on a small object to hold, such as a gift of dates for Eid.
Draw the net of a cuboid box big enough to hold it, marking the length, width and height.
Cut out and fold your net, then tape it into a box and check the object fits.
Work out the volume of your box using length × width × height. Decorate it if you like.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which 3D shape do you meet most often in daily life? What was the trickiest part of folding a net? How did building with unit cubes help you understand volume? Which activity taught you the most about faces, edges and vertices? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Apply Euler's Rule to Check Your Counting
rules.text: Apply Euler's rule (Vertices − Edges + Faces = 2) to check your counting.

rules.title: Euler's Formula: Vertices, Edges and Faces
rules.text: There is a beautiful pattern that connects these three numbers, discovered by a mathematician named Euler (say it 'Oiler'). For any solid with flat faces, if you take the number of vertices, subtract the number of edges, and add the number of faces, you always get 2. We write it as V − E + F = 2. For a cube: 8 − 12 + 6 = 2. It works! This little rule is a wonderful way to check your counting: if your three numbers do not give 2, you have miscounted somewhere and should count again.

rules.title: The Volume of a Cuboid Formula
rules.text: Because counting layer by layer always comes down to the same multiplication, we can write a rule. The volume of a cuboid = length × width × height. For our example, 4 × 3 × 3 = 36 cm³, exactly matching the cubes we counted. A cube is just a cuboid whose length, width and height are all equal, so the volume of a cube is one edge multiplied by itself three times. A cube of edge 2 cm has a volume of 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³.

rules.title: Worked Example: Testing a Square Pyramid
rules.text: Solution: Test with Euler's rule, V − E + F. That is 5 − 8 + 5 = 2. Because the answer is 2, her counting is consistent and correct. A square pyramid does indeed have 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices.

rules.title: Use Euler's Rule to Test a Shape
rules.text: Use Euler's rule (V − E + F = 2) to check whether a shape with 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces is possible. Which shape is it?

rules.title: Miscounting Hidden Parts
rules.text: Miscounting hidden parts. Some faces, edges and vertices hide round the back. Count in a fixed order and check with Euler's rule.

How many small 3 cm cubes fit inside a box that is 9 cm × 9 cm × 9 cm?
A net has 5 squares. Can it fold into a closed cube? Explain your answer.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: No – a closed cube needs exactly 6 faces, so 5 squares can only make an open cube.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: You stack 3 identical cubes in a tower. How many square faces are completely hidden where cubes touch, and how many are visible?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 4 hidden faces (2 touching joins × 2 faces each); total faces 3 × 6 = 18, so 18 − 4 = 14 visible.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Nets – Unfolding a Solid.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A net is a flat pattern that you can cut out and fold up to make a 3D shape. Here is the best way to picture it: imagine carefully unfolding a cardboard box until it lies completely flat on the table. That flat pattern of joined-up faces is the net of the box. Fold it back along the creases and it becomes a solid again. Every 3D shape with flat faces can be opened out into a net. Nets matter because they show the link between the flat 2D world and the solid 3D world. The number of shapes in a net tells you the number of faces the solid has — for example, a cube's net always has exactly 6 squares.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Drawing Solids and Seeing Different Views.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Drawing a solid shape on flat paper is a real challenge, because you must create the illusion that the shape has depth when the paper itself is flat. This is exactly what artists, architects and designers do every day, and there is a clever tool that makes it much easier: isometric paper. Isometric paper is covered with dots or lines arranged in a triangular pattern. Ordinary squared paper helps you draw flat squares and rectangles; isometric paper helps you draw cubes and cuboids that look solid. To draw a cube on isometric paper, you sketch three of its faces meeting at one corner along the dotted grid lines, so the flat drawing looks like it truly has depth.

rounds.explanation: A triangle is completely flat, so it is a 2D shape. Cubes, cylinders and cones are all solid 3D shapes.

selfAssessment: I can recognise that the same shape looks different from different viewpoints.
I can find the volume of a cube or cuboid by counting or multiplying unit cubes.
I can explain the difference between 2D and 3D shapes and give real examples of each.
I can name common 3D shapes: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere, prism and pyramid.
I can identify and count the faces, edges and vertices of a 3D shape.
I can describe the special properties of a cube (6 square faces, 12 equal edges, 8 vertices).
I can understand what a net is and identify which nets fold into a cube.
I can draw 3D shapes on isometric paper and show which faces are visible and which are hidden.
